1	In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright attitude of use, in which the insulated lid is uppermost. The described embodiments illustrate the invention and do not limit it. FIG. 1 through FIG. 5 show one carrier, each view showing the parts that view is concerned with, and a part introduced in one view is referred to elsewhere in this description whether or not it is shown in every view.
2	
3	## Overview of the carrier
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, a reusable passive cold-chain carrier includes an insulated outer shell 10, a removable product tray 20, a removable thermal module 40, and an insulated lid 60. The insulated outer shell 10 has a shell floor 12, shell side walls 14 rising from the shell floor 12, and an upper edge 16 at the top of the shell side walls 14. The insulated outer shell 10, the insulated lid 60, and the walls that bound the interior are of insulating construction, so that the carrier can be cleaned, stacked, and returned for reuse.
6	
7	Referring also to FIG. 4, the removable product tray 20 receives the payload. The removable product tray 20 has tray side walls 24 and tray feet 22. The tray feet 22 stand on the shell floor 12 and suspend the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12, so that a lower return passage 28 remains under the removable product tray 20. The tray side walls 24 are spaced inward from the shell side walls 14 to form two side supply passages 30, each side supply passage 30 extending upward from the lower return passage 28 alongside the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through the removable product tray 20.
8	
9	The removable product tray 20 lifts out of the insulated outer shell 10 as a unit, with the payload in it, once the removable thermal module 40 has been taken out. Loading and unloading therefore do not disturb the passages, because the passages are formed by the position that the removable product tray 20 takes up when it is returned to the insulated outer shell 10 and not by any separate ducting that has to be assembled.
10	
11	## The removable thermal module
12	
13	Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the removable thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 holding two opposed phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 is a self-supporting rigid frame body, stiff enough that the phase-change cassettes 44 it carries do not close the passages formed in it. The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.
14	
15	The rigid spacer frame 42 includes a central inlet opening 46 through its upper region, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the phase-change cassettes 44, and peripheral outlet openings 50. Each phase-change cassette 44 is a sealed cassette of phase-change material that is conditioned before use, and the two phase-change cassettes 44 are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening 46 with their faces mutually opposed. Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44 and opens at its lower end. The peripheral outlet openings 50 lie at the periphery of the rigid spacer frame 42 and are aligned with the side supply passages 30 when the removable thermal module 40 is in a registered position.
16	
17	Because the two phase-change cassettes 44 are opposed and are held apart by the rigid spacer frame 42, the air that enters between them is exposed to two cooled faces at once.
18	
19	## The registered passive circulation path
20	
21	The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow.
22	
23	In use, warm air rising from a product region within the removable product tray 20 enters the central inlet opening 46, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, descends through the downward guide ducts 48, enters the side supply passages 30, passes through the perforations 26 in the removable product tray 20, and returns through the lower return passage 28 to the product region. The path is closed on itself and surrounds the removable product tray 20 on the sides and underneath, so that cooled air reaches the payload around and beneath the removable product tray 20.
24	
25	The path exists only when the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. If the removable thermal module 40 is set down out of position, the peripheral outlet openings 50 discharge against the tray side walls 24 or against the shell side walls 14, the descending limb of the path is blocked, and the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box. This is the failure that the registration described below is directed to, and it is a failure that gives no outward sign, because a removable thermal module 40 that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.
26	
27	## Lid-driven registration and retention
28	
29	Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62, and the rigid spacer frame 42 has a mating channel 52 that receives the depending indexing rib 62. As the insulated lid 60 closes, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 52 and shifts the removable thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. The registration is therefore performed by the act of closing the carrier. The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position.
30	
31	A compressible lid gasket 64 on the insulated lid 60 seals against the upper edge 16 of the insulated outer shell 10 after registration. The order of these two events matters. The depending indexing rib 62 engages the mating channel 52 and completes the registration while the compressible lid gasket 64 is still clear of the upper edge 16, so that the removable thermal module 40 is free to be shifted by the depending indexing rib 62 and is not being asked to move after the interior has been closed off. Only then does continued closing compress the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 and seal the interior.
32	
33	The same closing movement presses resilient feet 54 of the rigid spacer frame 42 against ledges 18 of the insulated outer shell 10, so that the removable thermal module 40 cannot lift away from the removable product tray 20 during transport. That pressing holds the removable thermal module 40 down against handling, tilting, and vibration in transit, which would otherwise let the removable thermal module 40 rise and break the overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 50 and the side supply passages 30.
34	
35	Registration and retention are thus produced by the same movement that a user has to make in any event. Nothing has to be latched, clamped, or checked separately, and there is no state in which the carrier is closed and sealed but the circulation path is not established.
36	
37	## Condensate handling and the removable wick
38	
39	Referring to FIG. 2 and FIG. 4, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing in the bottom of the interior.
40	
41	The removable absorbent wick 72 has a pull tab 74. The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44 and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40. Routine servicing between journeys therefore does not require handling of the sealed phase-change cassettes 44, which are conditioned items that should be returned to conditioning intact. Withdrawing the removable absorbent wick 72 from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and placing a replacement absorbent wick in the shallow condensate channel 70 restores the carrier for the next journey.
42	
43	## Mechanical exposure indicator
44	
45	Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, the insulated outer shell 10 includes a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside. An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. A spring 86 acts on the indicator stem 82 in the outward direction and is held by the temperature-responsive latch 84 while the phase-change cassette 44 remains in condition.
46	
47	If that phase-change cassette 44 softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch 84, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette 44 cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The value of this behaviour is that a payload which was warmed part way through a journey and then cooled again arrives at a temperature that looks correct, and the contents alone give the recipient no way to know what happened. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 records the event in the structure of the carrier and holds the record until a person opens the carrier and deliberately resets it.
48	
49	The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. The circulation path is the same whether the indicator stem 82 is retained or has moved to the latched exposed position. The thermal condition being reported is taken directly from a phase-change cassette 44, that is, from the reserve that actually conditions the payload, and no electrical power, battery, or logging device is required for the indication.
50	
51	## Method of passively conditioning a payload
52	
53	In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes 44 are fitted to the rigid spacer frame 42 to form the removable thermal module 40, products are placed in the removable product tray 20, the removable product tray 20 is placed in the insulated outer shell 10 on its tray feet 22, the removable thermal module 40 is placed above the removable product tray 20, and the insulated lid 60 is closed. Closing the insulated lid 60 brings the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 52, shifts the removable thermal module 40 into the registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30, presses the resilient feet 54 against the ledges 18, and then compresses the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16. Air then circulates passively along the path described above for the duration of the journey.
54	
55	At the destination the insulated lid 60 is opened, the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out, and the removable product tray 20 is lifted out with the payload in it. Between journeys the removable absorbent wick 72 is withdrawn from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and replaced, the interior is cleaned, the phase-change cassettes 44 are returned for conditioning, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset by hand if it has moved to the latched exposed position.
56	
57	## Variations
58	
59	The removable absorbent wick 72 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features. A carrier may be built with the registered passive circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with either optional feature separately, or with both. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another where the combination is physically consistent. The claims that follow define the invention, and each claim is to be read in the light of the whole of this description.

The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.

The rigid spacer frame 42 includes a central inlet opening 46 through its upper region, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the phase-change cassettes 44, and peripheral outlet openings 50. Each phase-change cassette 44 is a sealed cassette of phase-change material that is conditioned before use, and the two phase-change cassettes 44 are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening 46 with their faces mutually opposed. Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44 and opens at its lower end. The peripheral outlet openings 50 lie at the periphery of the rigid spacer frame 42 and are aligned with the side supply passages 30 when the removable thermal module 40 is in a registered position.

Because the two phase-change cassettes 44 are opposed and are held apart by the rigid spacer frame 42, the air that enters between them is exposed to two cooled faces at once.

## The registered passive circulation path

The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow.

In use, warm air rising from a product region within the removable product tray 20 enters the central inlet opening 46, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, descends through the downward guide ducts 48, enters the side supply passages 30, passes through the perforations 26 in the removable product tray 20, and returns through the lower return passage 28 to the product region. The path is closed on itself and surrounds the removable product tray 20 on the sides and underneath, so that cooled air reaches the payload around and beneath the removable product tray 20.

The path exists only when the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. If the removable thermal module 40 is set down out of position, the peripheral outlet openings 50 discharge against the tray side walls 24 or against the shell side walls 14, the descending limb of the path is blocked, and the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box. This is the failure that the registration described below is directed to, and it is a failure that gives no outward sign, because a removable thermal module 40 that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.

## Lid-driven registration and retention

Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62, and the rigid spacer frame 42 has a mating channel 52 that receives the depending indexing rib 62. As the insulated lid 60 closes, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 52 and shifts the removable thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. The registration is therefore performed by the act of closing the carrier. The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position.

A compressible lid gasket 64 on the insulated lid 60 seals against the upper edge 16 of the insulated outer shell 10 after registration. The order of these two events matters. The depending indexing rib 62 engages the mating channel 52 and completes the registration while the compressible lid gasket 64 is still clear of the upper edge 16, so that the removable thermal module 40 is free to be shifted by the depending indexing rib 62 and is not being asked to move after the interior has been closed off. Only then does continued closing compress the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 and seal the interior.

The same closing movement presses resilient feet 54 of the rigid spacer frame 42 against ledges 18 of the insulated outer shell 10, so that the removable thermal module 40 cannot lift away from the removable product tray 20 during transport. That pressing holds the removable thermal module 40 down against handling, tilting, and vibration in transit, which would otherwise let the removable thermal module 40 rise and break the overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 50 and the side supply passages 30.

Registration and retention are thus produced by the same movement that a user has to make in any event. Nothing has to be latched, clamped, or checked separately, and there is no state in which the carrier is closed and sealed but the circulation path is not established.

## Condensate handling and the removable wick

Referring to FIG. 2 and FIG. 4, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing in the bottom of the interior.

The removable absorbent wick 72 has a pull tab 74. The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44 and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40. Routine servicing between journeys therefore does not require handling of the sealed phase-change cassettes 44, which are conditioned items that should be returned to conditioning intact. Withdrawing the removable absorbent wick 72 from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and placing a replacement absorbent wick in the shallow condensate channel 70 restores the carrier for the next journey.

## Mechanical exposure indicator

Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, the insulated outer shell 10 includes a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside. An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. A spring 86 acts on the indicator stem 82 in the outward direction and is held by the temperature-responsive latch 84 while the phase-change cassette 44 remains in condition.

If that phase-change cassette 44 softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch 84, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette 44 cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The value of this behaviour is that a payload which was warmed part way through a journey and then cooled again arrives at a temperature that looks correct, and the contents alone give the recipient no way to know what happened. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 records the event in the structure of the carrier and holds the record until a person opens the carrier and deliberately resets it.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. The circulation path is the same whether the indicator stem 82 is retained or has moved to the latched exposed position. The thermal condition being reported is taken directly from a phase-change cassette 44, that is, from the reserve that actually conditions the payload, and no electrical power, battery, or logging device is required for the indication.

## Method of passively conditioning a payload

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes 44 are fitted to the rigid spacer frame 42 to form the removable thermal module 40, products are placed in the removable product tray 20, the removable product tray 20 is placed in the insulated outer shell 10 on its tray feet 22, the removable thermal module 40 is placed above the removable product tray 20, and the insulated lid 60 is closed. Closing the insulated lid 60 brings the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 52, shifts the removable thermal module 40 into the registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30, presses the resilient feet 54 against the ledges 18, and then compresses the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16. Air then circulates passively along the path described above for the duration of the journey.

At the destination the insulated lid 60 is opened, the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out, and the removable product tray 20 is lifted out with the payload in it. Between journeys the removable absorbent wick 72 is withdrawn from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and replaced, the interior is cleaned, the phase-change cassettes 44 are returned for conditioning, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset by hand if it has moved to the latched exposed position.

## Variations

The removable absorbent wick 72 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features. A carrier may be built with the registered passive circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with either optional feature separately, or with both. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another where the combination is physically consistent. The claims that follow define the invention, and each claim is to be read in the light of the whole of this description.

1	Temperature-sensitive payloads such as medicines, diagnostic samples, and perishable foods are frequently distributed in insulated containers that carry their own thermal reserve. A container of this kind is loaded at a packing point, handed to one or more carriers, and opened at a destination that may be many hours away. Because the container travels unattended and often without electrical power, the thermal behaviour of the container has to be set at the moment of closing and cannot be corrected in transit.
2	
3	Two practical difficulties dominate the use of such containers. The first is the distribution of cold within the payload space. A thermal reserve placed against one wall, or laid directly on top of a payload, cools the material nearest to it strongly and the material farthest from it weakly, so the payload experiences a spread of temperatures. Direct contact between the thermal reserve and the payload can drive the contacted items below the intended range while more distant items drift above it. Moving air distributes the effect of the reserve more evenly, but a fan, pump, or other powered air mover adds a battery, a failure mode, and a service burden, and is unwelcome in a container that has to be washed, stacked, and returned.
4	
5	The second difficulty is that a container which relies on an internal air path only performs as intended if that path is actually present when the container is closed. Loose internal components are lifted, rotated, or nudged during loading and during transport. If the passages that are supposed to carry conditioned air downward are displaced relative to the passages that are supposed to carry it back, the intended path is broken and the container behaves as an ordinary insulated box, without any outward sign that anything is wrong. Placing that responsibility on the person who packs the container is unreliable, because a component that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.
6	
7	Related handling problems arise in reusable service. Condensate forms on cold surfaces inside a closed container and collects where it is difficult to reach. Removing it commonly means handling the thermal reserve itself, which is undesirable when the reserve is a sealed phase-change cassette that should not be opened in the field. Finally, a payload that has been briefly warmed can arrive at a temperature that appears correct, so a recipient inspecting the container at delivery cannot tell from the contents alone whether the thermal reserve lost its condition earlier in the journey.
8	
9	There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier in which the internal circulation path is established positively by the act of closing the container, in which the thermal reserve is held in that established relationship during transport, and in which routine servicing and evidence of thermal exposure are available without opening the thermal reserve.

content.content:
1	A reusable passive cold-chain carrier has an insulated shell, a removable product tray, a removable thermal module, and an insulated lid. Tray feet leave a return passage beneath the tray, whose side walls are spaced inward from the shell side walls to form two side supply passages. The module is a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes and having a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts, and peripheral outlet openings. As the lid closes, a depending indexing rib enters a mating channel in the frame and shifts the module into a registered position in which the outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. Air circulates without a powered air mover, rising from the product region into the inlet opening, descending the guide ducts into the side supply passages, and returning through tray perforations and the return passage.
